strengths: The proposed defense is training-free and operates entirely at inference time without requiring retraining of the underlying reconstruction network, successfully preserving clean reconstruction quality.

The defense is grounded in physical principles (cyclic measurement consistency), exploiting the structure of the MRI forward model to naturally detect and mitigate perturbations that are overfitted to the acquired k-space locations.

The evaluation is highly comprehensive, covering multiple datasets (fastMRI knee and brain), several popular unrolled architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, VarNets), various attack types (l_infinity, l_2, l_0 spikes), and challenging settings like blind mitigation.

The authors rigorously evaluate their defense against adaptive attacks (where the attacker has full knowledge of the defense strategy) and prove that the iterative version of their defense remains highly robust.
weaknesses: The method incurs a noticeable computational overhead at inference time because it relies on an optimization-based defense (reverse PGD) that requires multiple iterations (e.g., 100+ iterations for convergence, as shown in Table 2). The paper lacks a detailed discussion or comparison of the absolute runtime (in seconds/minutes per slice) of the proposed iterative scheme.

The paper lacks comparison against other test-time purification/mitigation methods, such as diffusion-based purification (e.g., Alkhouri et al., 2024), which also do not require retraining the reconstruction network.

The explanation directly below Theorem 1 requires refinement: the theorem bounds the error on the acquired locations, but to conclude that the error on the unacquired locations (the complement set) is large, one must explicitly assume that the adversarial attack was successful (i.e., that the overall reconstruction error is large).
It is unclear how the synthesized masks are generated for non-uniform/random undersampling patterns (Section D.8), as the main text only describes shifting equispaced patterns by one line.

strengths: Proposes a novel training-free, test-time purification strategy utilizing cyclic measurement consistency, which avoids the performance trade-offs on clean images associated with adversarial training.

Provides a solid theoretical foundation (Theorem 1) explaining how adversarial perturbations in the acquired k-space propagate as large residuals in the unacquired regions, justifying the use of cyclic consistency.
Thoroughly evaluates the defense against adaptive attacks following standard security guidelines, confirming that the defense is robust and does not rely on gradient obfuscation.
Demonstrates excellent generalizability across various deep learning reconstruction architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, E2E-VarNet, Recurrent-VarNet) and fastMRI datasets.
Introduces a practical and clinically motivated sparse/bounded attack model representing k-space spikes that cause herringbone artifacts, showing the method's real-world utility.
weaknesses: High computational overhead during inference: Since the mitigation algorithm requires iterative optimization (e.g., around 100 iterations of reverse PGD) involving multiple forward/backward passes through already expensive unrolled networks, it significantly slows down the reconstruction process.
The 'blind' mitigation scenario further exacerbates this computational cost, as it requires a nested search/scheduling of the hyperparameters epsilon and alpha.

The mask synthesis relies on generating a new sampling pattern delta from the same distribution as the acquisition mask omega, which is shown for Cartesian grids but may be non-trivial to extend to complex non-Cartesian trajectories (radial, spiral) used in clinical practice.

strengths: The proposed defense is completely training-free, which avoids the high computational cost of adversarial training and prevents the degradation of reconstruction performance on clean, non-perturbed inputs.

The method has strong theoretical underpinnings. Theorem 1 provides a mathematical characterization of how adversarial perturbations propagate to the unacquired k-space locations, justifying the use of cyclic consistency.

The paper includes a thorough evaluation against adaptive attacks (following Carlini & Wagner / Athalye guidelines). The authors unroll the defense for up to 100 steps to generate strong adaptive attacks and verify that gradient obfuscation does not occur.

The proposed method is shown to be highly generalizable, performing well across multiple datasets (fastMRI knee and brain), different acceleration rates, and five distinct physics-driven deep learning reconstruction network architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, E2E-VarNet, Recurrent-VarNet).

The connection made between adversarial perturbations and clinical herringbone artifacts (modeled as sparse l_0 k-space spikes) is highly original and demonstrates the practical utility of the defense in medical imaging hardware failures.
weaknesses: The primary bottleneck of the proposed method is its computational overhead at inference time. Since the defense relies on iterative optimization (reverse PGD) over multiple synthesized undersampling patterns, it requires numerous forward and backward passes through the reconstruction network. The manuscript lacks a quantitative discussion of the exact reconstruction time per slice/volume, which is critical for real-time or clinically feasible MRI workflows.

The paper lacks comparison with other test-time purification defenses. While it compares extensively against training-based robust methods (AT, SMUG), comparing with test-time purification baselines (such as diffusion-based purification or simple input-space denoising) would make the evaluation more comprehensive.

The joint optimization of parameters in the blind setup (described in Section 3.2 and Appendix E) relies on heuristic linear schedulers for epsilon and alpha. The sensitivity of the reconstruction quality and convergence stability to the choice of these initial scheduler parameters is not fully explored.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel, training-free approach for mitigating adversarial attacks in physics-driven DL-based MRI reconstruction by leveraging cyclic measurement consistency.

The theoretical foundation is solid; Theorem 3.1 rigorously explains how adversarial perturbations propagate to the unacquired k-space regions, providing a clear mathematical justification for why cyclic consistency works as a mitigation objective.

The experimental evaluation is highly comprehensive, covering multiple datasets (knee and brain), various unrolled network architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, VarNets), different undersampling patterns, and competitive baselines (including adversarial training, SMUG, and diffusion purification).
The paper includes critical evaluations against adaptive attacks and blind mitigation scenarios, which are essential for showing the practical security and viability of the defense.
The connection to real-world herringbone artifacts via sparse and bounded k-space perturbations adds strong clinical relevance to the study.
weaknesses: The primary limitation of the proposed method is its high computational cost during inference. As shown in Table 3, the inference time increases from ~0.04 minutes to 6.78 minutes, and memory usage goes up to 21.3 GB (or up to 66.5 GB for dynamic MRI). This could limit its applicability in real-time clinical workflows.

The alternating optimization strategy used for blind mitigation (finding optimum epsilon and alpha) introduces extra hyperparameters and might be sensitive to the choice of schedulers across different datasets or scanner configurations.

strengths: Innovative training-free defense mechanism for physics-driven DL reconstruction based on the concept of cyclic consistency, avoiding the heavy computational burden of adversarial training and the risk of degrading clean reconstruction quality.
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation against state-of-the-art defenses, including adversarial training, SMUG, randomized smoothing, and diffusion-based purification.
Strong evaluation under adaptive attacks, which includes careful tuning of the adversary and verifying the avoidance of gradient obfuscation (satisfying the Carlini & Wagner guidelines).

Well-motivated theory (Theorem 3.1) showing why adversarial attacks primarily affect the unacquired k-space complement, providing a solid physical intuition for the proposed cyclic consistency defense.
A highly practical and creative connection to real-world medical artifacts (herringbone artifacts modeled as sparse k-space spike attacks).
weaknesses: High computational overhead at inference time: Tab. 3 shows that the proposed defense requires 6.78 minutes per slice and 21.3 GB of memory. This is significantly slower than standard reconstruction and might limit clinical feasibility where real-time or fast batch processing is required.

The generation of synthesized masks $\{\Delta_k\}$ is straightforward for Cartesian equispaced trajectories (shifting by one line), but it is less clear how easily and effectively this strategy scales to complex non-Cartesian trajectories (e.g., radial, spiral) that are also common in accelerated MRI.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel, training-free defense mechanism for physics-driven deep learning MRI reconstruction by leveraging cyclic measurement consistency.

The theoretical foundation (Theorem 3.1) is solid, providing a mathematical explanation for why adversarial perturbations mainly corrupt unacquired k-space locations, thereby breaking consistency with synthesized subsampling masks.

The evaluation is highly comprehensive, spanning multiple MRI datasets (fastMRI knee and brain), several popular unrolled architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, E2E-VarNet, Recurrent VarNet), and different attack types (including a practical modeling of herringbone artifacts as $\ell_0$ perturbations).

The defense against adaptive attacks is thoroughly validated. The authors demonstrate that if an adaptive attacker attempts to bypass the defense by forcing cyclic consistency, they are physically constrained to produce a high-quality reconstruction, meaning the defense remains robust.
weaknesses: The primary drawback is the extreme computational overhead during inference. The proposed test-time optimization requires around 100 iterations of reverse PGD, resulting in an inference time of 6.78 minutes per slice (Table 3). This is a major bottleneck that makes the method clinically impractical for real-time or routine 3D/4D MRI workflows.

The memory footprint during inference is exceptionally high, requiring 21.3 GB for 2D and up to 66.5 GB for dynamic MRI reconstructions. This restricts the deployment of the defense on typical clinical scanners or standard hospital workstation GPUs.

The blind mitigation strategy relies on heuristic scheduling to jointly tune $\epsilon$ and $\alpha$ (Figure 14). While effective on the tested datasets, this adds additional hyperparameters that may be sensitive to variations in SNR, contrast, or scanner hardware.

The method inherently depends on the quality of the underlying pre-trained reconstruction model. As shown in the ablation study (Table 17), if the baseline model is sub-optimal or early-stopped, the mitigation can only recover image quality up to that sub-optimal baseline's clean limit.
